title: Five of Wands: Give different efforts rules they can work with

quickTake.upright: Everyone is making an effort; first find out what the contest is about.
quickTake.reversed: Differences may be avoided, or the argument may be getting more tangled.

bodyMarkdown:
Upright in one sentence: Everyone is making an effort; first find out what the contest is about.

Reversed in one sentence: Differences may be avoided, or the argument may be getting more tangled.

Five people each hold a staff and make large movements, but it is hard to see a shared direction. The Five of Wands' most useful question is not “Who will win?” but “Are these efforts going toward the same thing?”

## Five people exert themselves without a shared direction

Under a blue sky, five people in short garments of different colors and patterns stand on uneven ground. One holds a staff upright, another lifts one over a shoulder, and another reaches diagonally toward the middle. Five long staffs cross in the air. The foreground figure has their back to us; the others' bodies and gazes do not all face the same way either.

There is no blood in the picture and no clear leader occupying the center. The crossed staffs may suggest an argument, but the scene could also resemble training or a game. The image alone cannot establish everyone's intentions, much less turn every difference of opinion into hostility. Different clothing is a visible fact; different goals are an interpretation that needs checking.

The crossed staffs crowd the picture, yet we can still distinguish where each person stands on the ground. That contrast is useful: views can collide, but participants still need to know where they stand and at what point they can step out. A lack of shared direction in the picture does not mean disagreement must be eliminated. Sometimes stating each person's aim turns disorder into an exercise that can be deliberately structured. But if intimidation or harm is already present in real life, Waite's mention of a mock fight does not justify dismissing the problem as ordinary adjustment.

## Understanding competition through a mock fight

Waite describes a group who may be engaged in sport or strife, explicitly using the idea of a mock fight. He also connects the card with competition and efforts to achieve results. The Five of Wands' historical themes therefore extend beyond interpersonal quarrels to practice and striving to get ahead.

The old book's reversed meanings mention disputes, litigation, and contradiction. This article retains the need to address disagreement but does not use those meanings to predict legal trouble. What follows about discussion rules, learning to work together, and conflict avoidance is an original modern learning application.

## Understanding the upright card

Upright, the card can reveal a situation that has not yet been coordinated. Someone values speed, someone else values quality, and someone wants their proposal to be noticed. If people are discussing different levels of the problem, greater effort may cause more collisions. Clarify goals, resources, and criteria separately so that disagreement can produce useful information.

Competition with rules can also help people practice. You can compare methods, test ideas, and hear objections without turning winning or losing into a judgment of a person's worth. The essentials are that participants know the rules, can express different views, and can identify a next step after the discussion.

## Understanding the reversed card

Here the reversal suggests two checks: has conflict been pushed out of sight, or has it become exhausting with no way forward? If nobody openly objects but everyone acts on a different understanding, the problem remains. Repeatedly arguing over the same sentence is not necessarily a serious comparison of options either.

Temporarily narrow the topic, address one observable disagreement, and agree on what information will decide it. If there are specific threats or disrespectful behavior, respond to the actual behavior and seek appropriate support. “This is a necessary adjustment” should not require you to keep enduring it.

Both upright and reversed cards can involve arguments; loudness need not be the distinction. A better question is whether disagreement creates new information: what did the discussion teach you, who can decide, and can everyone accept the rules? Upright in an obstacle position may show competition crowding out cooperation. Reversed in an advice position may invite someone to release an unnecessary need to win, rather than always give way.

## A band rehearsal does not need everyone to win

**Original fictional example.** Five members of an amateur band are preparing for a community performance. The guitarist wants to add a solo, the singer worries the song will be too long, and the drummer wants a faster tempo. Everyone prepares seriously, but each discussion becomes a popularity vote. Their question is: “How can we stop arguing about the arrangement at every rehearsal?” The upright Five of Wands appears in the position for the current state of cooperation.

Five staffs reach into the middle at once, like several worthwhile ideas competing for the same stretch of time. No clear conductor appears in the image, suggesting that this reading should first ask about decision rules instead of singling out a “difficult person.” Waite's mock fight offers another angle: replace the argument with brief trial performances, testing different methods against the same goal. Enthusiasm can become useful material, provided everyone knows what they are trying to solve.

If the real disagreement is that someone cannot accept the performance repertoire, trial runs cannot replace a discussion of their willingness to participate. If the budget or equipment cannot support an arrangement, rule out the impractical options first. Objections sometimes introduce necessary limits rather than obstructing creativity.

They first agree on the length of the performance, then try each of two versions once, recording them to compare only transitions and how they sound. A person chosen in advance finalizes the version submitted to the organizers, while other ideas wait for the next rehearsal. The argument gains a way forward without growing into judgments about character.

## Why is everyone doing their own thing when nobody objects?

**Original fictional example.** A group of friends takes turns leading a book club. They rarely seem to argue, but on three occasions someone has pulled out at the last minute. Some want serious discussion of the text, while others just want a relaxed chat. The hosts never ask further because they fear upsetting the atmosphere. Their question is: “How should the book club handle everyone saying they don't mind?” The reversed Five of Wands appears in the hidden-obstacle position.

Thinking of the crossed staffs as different purposes that have not yet been voiced offers a modern reversed reading: conflict may not have disappeared; it may have lost the chance to be openly coordinated. The known differences in goals support this interpretation, but a last-minute absence by itself does not prove disrespect. The point of the reading is to let needs be spoken, not to create fresh accusations.

It is also possible that everyone shares the same goals but the timing has recently been inconvenient. If questions reveal specific scheduling conflicts behind the absences, change the date. If someone clearly wants to withdraw, continuing to demand their input makes little sense. “Not joining this round” needs to be an acceptable option.

Before the next meeting, the host asks what everyone hopes to get from the hour and proposes a trial: text discussion in the first half, free conversation in the second. After two meetings, they gather feedback again. Anyone who dislikes this format can skip it rather than using silence to express disagreement.

## A small exercise

Recall a disagreement and write down each side's proposed solution and the need behind it. Then write a sentence you can check: “Are we actually trying to solve … and … respectively?” Check your understanding first, without asking the other person to agree with you yet.

## Common misreadings

The Five of Wands does not automatically mean someone is targeting you, nor does it guarantee that every argument is healthy competition. Check actual behavior and rules before deciding whether this is useful adjustment, a mismatch of goals, or a draining struggle that should stop.
